title: Olympic Code versus Village Art
bigQuestion: What does an art gain and lose when it rewrites its rules for the Olympic stage, and why do some arts choose to stay off it?

story.title: One Word, Two Arenas
story.kicker: A festival ring of sawdust and an Olympic mat both use the word wrestling, and almost nothing else is shared.
paragraphs: In a Swiss mountain town, two wrestlers in short canvas trousers face each other in a ring of sawdust. Thousands of people sit on wooden stands. The prize for the champion of the national festival is a live bull. The rules come from the *Schwingen* federation founded in Switzerland in 1895.

Far away, two wrestlers step onto a round Olympic mat under bright lights. They wear singlets in the colors of an international federation. A clock counts down each period, and judges enter points into a computer. The rules come from United World Wrestling, which writes one code for every country.

Both events are called wrestling in English, but they answer to different institutions. The Swiss festival serves a regional community, its music, its food and its long memory. The Olympic bout serves a world audience that needs the same rules, gear and times in every country. Each set of rules makes sense for the room it belongs to.

This chapter looks at what the Olympic stage asks for: electric scoring in fencing, blue jackets in judo, bare heads in men's boxing and a near loss for wrestling in 2013. Then it visits arts that kept their own rooms, from Swiss sawdust rings to Icelandic belts, Indian earth pits and Japanese kendo halls.
story.think: Is a sport that changes its rules for television still the same sport? Who should get to decide?

lessons.title: Fencing Plugs In
lessons.mainIdea: Olympic fencing moved to electric scoring one weapon at a time, from épée in 1936 to sabre in 1988, so judges could see touches too fast for the eye.
reading: Fencing has been part of every modern Summer Olympics since 1896. Its world body, the Fédération Internationale d'Escrime, or FIE, was founded in Paris in 1913. For decades, a jury of judges watched each bout and voted on whether a touch had landed. Touches with a light blade are often too fast to see clearly.

In 1936 at the Berlin Olympics, épée became the first weapon scored with an *electric scoring* apparatus. A wire ran from each fencer's weapon to a box that lit a lamp when a touch arrived. Foil followed at the 1956 Melbourne Games, and sabre at the 1988 Seoul Games. Each weapon needed its own jacket and wiring rules.

The machines made results easier to check and harder to dispute. They also changed the look of a bout, with fencers tied to reels by cords. Some older masters said the change rewarded speed over form. The FIE's *standardization*, making gear the same everywhere, became the price of a scoreboard every audience could read.

words.d: a system in which a touch closes a circuit and lights a lamp on a scoring box
making gear, sizes or rules the same everywhere
the Fédération Internationale d'Escrime, the world fencing body founded in Paris in 1913

check.q: Which fencing weapon was scored electrically first at the Olympics?

check.why: Judges voting by eye often disagreed on very fast touches.

lessons.title: A Blue Jacket in Judo
lessons.mainIdea: The International Judo Federation added a blue jacket for one athlete in the late 1990s, so viewers could tell two players apart.
reading: In Kanō Jigorō's Kodokan, judo players wore white jackets, and many Japanese teachers saw white as part of the art. For decades, Olympic judo followed that custom. One player wore a red or white belt marker so judges could tell them apart. On television, two white jackets tangled together were hard to follow.

Anton Geesink of the Netherlands, who won the open-weight gold medal in Tokyo in 1964, pressed for a colored jacket. The International Judo Federation approved the *blue judogi* in the late 1990s. It was used at the Olympic Games for the first time in Sydney in 2000. One athlete now wears white and the other blue.

The change drew objections from judo leaders in Japan, who argued for the white jacket. Supporters answered that a world sport needs to be readable by viewers and judges. The debate showed two institutions with different aims. The Kodokan guards a teaching tradition, while the IJF runs a *televised* world competition.

words.d: the jacket and trousers worn for judo
a blue judo uniform, used for one athlete in IJF events and first at the Olympics in 2000
shown on television to viewers far from the event

lessons.title: Headgear Comes Off
lessons.mainIdea: Olympic boxing added headgear in 1984 and removed it for men in 2016, showing that equipment rules follow the governing body's aims.
reading: Amateur boxers at the Olympics fought without head protection for decades. *Headgear*, a padded guard for the head, became required at the 1984 Los Angeles Games. Amateur boxing leaders said it would lower injuries. For the next thirty years, the padded head was part of how people recognized Olympic boxing.

In 2013 the world amateur boxing body, AIBA, ruled that elite men would compete without headgear. The Rio de Janeiro Games in 2016 were the first Olympics since 1980 in which men boxed without it. Women kept the headgear at Rio. AIBA cited its own medical review, and some doctors disagreed with its reading of the evidence.

The headgear story shows how a *governing body* shapes a sport through its gear rules. Removing the guard also made Olympic bouts look more like professional boxing. That mattered as the body opened Olympic boxing to professional fighters in 2016. Equipment rules carry choices about safety, audience and the sport's image.

words.d: a padded guard worn on the head in some combat sports
an organization that writes and enforces the rules of a sport
the world amateur boxing body that ran Olympic boxing through 2016

check.why: Headgear became required at the 1984 Los Angeles Games.

lessons.title: Wrestling Nearly Leaves, 2013
lessons.mainIdea: In 2013 the IOC's executive board moved to drop wrestling from the Olympics, and the sport changed its leaders and rules to win its place back.
reading: Wrestling was part of the ancient Olympic Games and of the first modern Games in 1896. On February 12, 2013, the IOC Executive Board recommended dropping it from the 2020 program. The *Olympic program* is the list of sports and events at a Games. Wrestling fans in Iran, the United States and Russia joined in protest.

The world wrestling body, then called FILA, changed quickly. Its president resigned that month, and Nenad Lalović of Serbia took over. The federation added more women's weight classes and changed scoring rules to reward action. It also gave athletes and women a larger voice in its leadership.

On September 8, 2013, IOC members meeting in Buenos Aires voted wrestling back onto the program for 2020 and 2024. In 2014 FILA renamed itself United World Wrestling. The episode showed that even the oldest Olympic sport keeps its place only by meeting the IOC's current tests. A *reform* is a planned change meant to fix a problem.

words.d: the list of sports and events held at an Olympic Games
a planned change meant to fix a problem
the world wrestling body, called FILA until 2014

check.why: FILA became United World Wrestling in 2014.

lessons.title: Sumo in Two Codes
lessons.mainIdea: Sumo lives under two codes: professional sumo in Japan with its ranks and rituals, and amateur sumo with weight classes run by a world federation.
reading: Professional sumo in Japan is run by the *Japan Sumo Association*. Its six yearly tournaments, its ranks up to yokozuna and its Shinto-linked ring ceremonies make it a Japanese institution. Wrestlers live in stables and follow the association's rules on dress and daily life. There are no weight classes in professional sumo.

The International Sumo Federation was founded in 1992 to spread *amateur sumo* around the world. It holds world championships and divides wrestlers into weight classes, like Olympic wrestling. It also runs women's events, which professional sumo does not have. Sumo has appeared at the World Games, a multi-sport event for sports outside the Olympics.

The two codes answer different questions. Professional sumo answers to a Japanese audience and a long tradition of ranks and ceremony. Amateur sumo answers to national federations that need a sport they can teach and judge anywhere. Amateur leaders have sought Olympic recognition, and sumo is not on the Olympic program.

words.d: the body that runs professional sumo in Japan
sumo run by the International Sumo Federation, with weight classes and women's events

lessons.title: A Stage for Other Sports
lessons.mainIdea: The World Games, first held in 1981, gave sports outside the Olympic program, including several martial arts, their own international stage.
reading: The Olympic program has limited room, and many governing bodies want a place on it. In 1980 a group of international federations formed what is now the International World Games Association. The first *World Games* were held in Santa Clara, California, in 1981. They are held every four years, usually the year after a Summer Olympics.

The World Games have included martial arts and combat sports that were not on the Olympic program, such as sumo, ju-jitsu, kickboxing and Muaythai. Karate appeared there for years before its single Olympic appearance in Tokyo. For many federations, the World Games are a place to show that they can run a fair international event.

The World Games work under IOC *patronage*, meaning official support without full Olympic status. They use existing venues in a host city rather than building a new Olympic park. For smaller arts, the Games give television time, funding reasons for national teams and a record of results. They also require the same standard rules that the Olympics do.

words.d: a multi-sport event for sports outside the Olympic program, first held in 1981
official support given by a larger body
a competition that brings many different sports together in one host city

lessons.title: Sawdust and a Bull
lessons.mainIdea: Swiss Schwingen is run by a national federation founded in 1895 for a festival culture, and it has never sought an Olympic place.
reading: *Schwingen* is a form of Swiss folk wrestling with roots in the Alpine farming regions. Wrestlers wear short trousers of heavy canvas over their clothes, a garment used only for this sport. Bouts take place in a round ring covered with sawdust. Village and regional festivals held matches long before any national body existed.

The Eidgenössischer Schwingerverband, the Swiss wrestling federation, was founded in 1895. It organizes the national festival, held every three years, where the champion is named Schwingerkönig, king of the wrestlers. The best-known prize is a live bull. The festival also includes alphorn music and flag throwing.

The federation writes rules for Swiss rings, not for world television. It has no weight classes, and its heroes are often farmers, butchers and carpenters. The national festival draws tens of thousands of spectators. Its *festival culture* is the institution it answers to, and the Olympic stage would ask it to change what it protects.

words.d: Swiss folk wrestling, held in a ring of sawdust
'king of the wrestlers,' the title of the champion at the Swiss national festival
the music, food, games and customs that surround a community celebration

lessons.title: Glíma and the Grettir Belt
lessons.mainIdea: Iceland's glíma was shown at the 1912 Stockholm Olympics but stayed a national sport, with its own belt trophy and its own rules.
reading: *Glíma* is Iceland's traditional wrestling. Old Icelandic sagas mention wrestling contests, and glíma has been treated as a national sport since the late 1800s. Wrestlers wear special leather belts, and the rules stress upright posture and fair conduct. Icelandic clubs still hold glíma contests each year, and the sport keeps a small, steady following.

In 1912 a team of Icelandic wrestlers gave a glíma demonstration at the Stockholm Olympics. A *demonstration sport* is shown at a Games without official medals. Iceland was then under Danish rule, and the display helped show Icelandic identity to a world audience. Glíma did not return to the Olympic program.

At home, glíma's top contest is the fight for the Grettir Belt, named after Grettir, a strong hero of an Icelandic saga. The contest dates to the early 1900s. The Icelandic Glíma Association governs the sport today. Its rules serve a small nation's schools and clubs and its sense of a shared past.

lessons.title: Earth Pit and Mat in India
lessons.mainIdea: Indian pehlwani grew in earthen akhara pits, and Indian wrestlers moved onto Olympic mats, winning India's first individual Olympic medal in 1952.
reading: *Pehlwani* is a form of wrestling long practiced in north India and Pakistan. Wrestlers train in an *akhara*, a training ground with a pit of soft earth, often under one senior teacher. Many akharas follow a strict daily life with shared meals and exercise. Matches called dangal are held at fairs and festivals, often on earth, with prizes from local patrons.

Pehlwani wrestlers gained fame abroad in the early 1900s. Ghulam Mohammad Baksh, known as the Great Gama, traveled to London in 1910 and wrestled the Polish champion Stanisław Zbyszko. Gama became a hero across South Asia. His fame came from challenge matches, not from any Olympic event.

Olympic wrestling needed a mat, a clock and weight classes. Khashaba Dadasaheb Jadhav of Maharashtra won a freestyle bronze medal at the 1952 Helsinki Games. It was independent India's first individual Olympic medal. Today many Indian wrestlers train on both earth and mats, moving between two institutions with different rules.

a traditional training ground for wrestlers, with a pit of soft earth
a wrestling contest held at a fair or festival in South Asia

lessons.title: Kendo Keeps Its Own Hall
lessons.mainIdea: Kendo built national and world federations after 1952 but has kept away from the Olympic program to protect its own ways of judging.
reading: Kendo is Japanese fencing with bamboo swords and armor. After 1945 the occupation restricted it in Japanese schools. The All Japan Kendo Federation was founded in 1952. In 1970 national bodies formed the International Kendo Federation, and the first World Kendo Championships were held in Tokyo that year.

Kendo judging looks for more than a touch. Referees award a point only when a strike lands with correct spirit, posture and follow-through, a standard called *yūkō-datotsu*, a valid strike. The rule asks referees to judge the whole action. That makes kendo hard to score with machines like the ones fencing adopted.

Kendo leaders in Japan have long said they do not seek a place on the Olympic program. They argue that chasing medals could push the art toward scoring points instead of training character. Kendo still has ranks, a world federation and world championships. It shows that an art can be international and organized while choosing a *non-Olympic* path.

words.d: Japanese fencing with bamboo swords and armor
a valid strike in kendo, judged on spirit, posture and follow-through as well as contact
organized as a sport but not part of the Olympic program
